tldr: By repurposing the same pretrained trajectory diffusion model in two roles—as a smart ego planner and as an adversary scenario generator that corners the ego vehicle—this work shows that high-precision driving and weakness validation via safety-critical scenarios can be achieved simultaneously.
hero_caption: Overall framework of the proposed approach. Based on features extracted from a shared scene encoder, the ego planner and adversary decoders are sampled independently. Guidance gradients from energy functions such as Time-to-Collision (TTC) and hard braking are applied to the adversary, generating realistic yet aggressive behaviors.
overview:
Autonomous motion planning demands two capabilities: generating safe, human-like trajectories that account for interactions with surrounding vehicles, and validating robustness so the vehicle does not fail even in rare, hazardous situations. However, standard imitation learning tends to learn only average safe driving, smoothing out multiple behavioral modes. Furthermore, existing datasets consist mostly of everyday driving logs, making it difficult to evaluate models on harsh long-tail (extremely rare, safety-critical) situations.

To address this, the authors turned to Diffusion Probabilistic Models (DPMs), which excel at multi-modal future prediction. Leveraging the ability to steer (guide) trajectories using energy function gradients during reverse-diffusion sampling, they proposed an approach that assigns two complementary roles to a single model: guiding the ego vehicle toward rules such as target speed to act as a high-performance planner, and guiding surrounding vehicles to raise collision risk to act as a safety-critical scenario generator.

In closed-loop evaluations on the large-scale autonomous driving benchmark nuPlan, the planner equipped with the newly proposed SSDS decoder substantially outperformed conventional baselines, especially in challenging settings with dense traffic interactions. On the other hand, when subjected to aggressive cut-in and hard-braking scenarios generated by the exact same model, planners with higher benchmark scores experienced a much sharper drop in performance. They failed to take lateral evasive maneuvers and ended up rear-ending vehicles, exposing critical weaknesses that remain hidden under standard benchmark evaluations.
contributions: Established a unified framework that utilizes the same pretrained diffusion model in two complementary roles: as an ego motion planner and as an adversarial safety-critical scenario generator in closed loop.
Proposed the Single-Stream Dual-Stream (SSDS) transformer decoder inspired by video generation models, deeply and symmetrically fusing scene context and trajectory tokens.
Devised the DAPSE guidance scheme, enabling zero-shot steering using arbitrary energy functions in clean trajectory space without post-hoc training or auxiliary networks.

Demonstrated that closed-loop safety-critical scenarios that push the planner's evasive limits while preserving realism can be generated through combined guidance of TTC (Time-to-Collision), lane changes, and rapid deceleration.

sections.heading: Can One Model Handle Both Driving and Attacking?
sections.summary: Autonomous driving requires both human-like trajectory planning and safety evaluation under long-tail extreme scenarios. This paper proposes a new framework that leverages the same diffusion model trained on future traffic trajectory distributions as both a planner and an aggressive test scenario generator via inference-time guidance.
sections.details:
Developing learning-based planners for autonomous vehicles faces two major hurdles. One is planning safe, human-like trajectories within traffic that intricately interacts with surrounding vehicles. The other is correctly evaluating whether the system can safely cope with dangerous situations that rarely occur in the real world.

Standard imitation learning approaches trained on expert driving data tend to 'mode-average' human diverse choices into a single output. Furthermore, existing benchmarks are dominated by everyday, benign driving logs, so achieving high scores does not guarantee robustness in extreme situations.

The authors realized that both of these challenges can be tackled with a single diffusion probabilistic model (DPM). Diffusion models can not only represent the joint distribution of future trajectories of the ego vehicle and surrounding vehicles multi-modally, but also flexibly steer (guide) trajectories at inference time using gradients of energy functions without retraining the model. In other words, guiding toward lower energy (safe, comfortable, traffic-rule compliant) yields a high-performance 'planner', while guiding surrounding agents toward higher risk for the ego vehicle turns it into an 'adversarial scenario generator'.

The specific contributions of this paper are threefold. First, the 'SSDS-DiT decoder', which adopts the architecture of modern video generation models, enhances the fusion of environmental context and trajectories. Second, they propose 'DAPSE', a sampling scheme that strictly reflects arbitrary energy functions without retraining. Third, they realize safety-critical scenario generation that induces sudden cut-ins and hard braking without sacrificing realism in nuPlan closed-loop environments.

Guidance gradients that elevate collision risk and other factors are applied to adversaries, which are interactively simulated with the environment via an LQR controller.

sections.heading: From Limitations of Imitation Learning to Diffusion Models and Critical Scenarios
sections.summary: We review the issues of conventional planning methods and imitation learning, confirming the superiority of diffusion models in trajectory prediction and planning. Furthermore, this study positions itself as generating realistic, closed-loop, high-speed adversarial scenarios, contrasting with conventional open-loop-focused scenario generation methods.
sections.details:
### Evolution of Data-Driven Motion Planning
Conventional local planners relied on hand-crafted rules, sampling, and Model Predictive Control (MPC), but tended to get trapped in local optima in dense, unpredictable urban environments. In contrast, imitation learning (IL), which implicitly learns driving rules from large-scale expert data, became widespread. However, simple regression-based imitation learning averages out multiple valid behavioral candidates, producing unnatural behaviors.

### Rise of Diffusion Models in Trajectory Generation
Diffusion models have been introduced to robot control and autonomous driving as a powerful approach to directly capture complex, multi-modal trajectory distributions while avoiding this averaging problem. In particular, recent works like Diffusion Planner use Diffusion Transformers (DiT) to simultaneously generate trajectories for both the ego and surrounding vehicles, achieving success with a framework that unifies upstream prediction and downstream planning.

### Safety-Critical Scenario Generation
To properly stress-test planners, extreme conditions absent from regular driving logs must be automatically generated. However, early adversarial generation methods (such as AdvSim) focused solely on causing planner failure, often resulting in physically impossible, unnatural behaviors. Subsequently, methods leveraging learned traffic priors to preserve realism (STRIVE) and diffusion-guided approaches (SafeSim) emerged, but these were constrained to intersection-focused or open-loop evaluations.

This study stands apart by targeting high-speed regimes such as highways and combining the diffusion model's own generative capability with interpretable energy function guidance to generate safety-critical scenarios with tight reaction times, such as sudden cut-ins and hard braking, in a closed loop.

sections.heading: Representing Multi-Agent Future Trajectories with a Joint Diffusion Model
sections.summary: We explain the formulation of the diffusion model that represents the future trajectories of the ego and surrounding vehicles as a single tensor and performs noise addition and denoising. The model is trained to predict clean trajectories for all agents in one go from noise while incorporating scene context.
sections.details:
In this study, future motions of the ego vehicle and surrounding other vehicles are handled together in a single diffusion model.

First, current scene context $\mathbf{E_{f}}$ includes current and past state histories of each agent, lane polylines including traffic light states, static obstacles, and the ego vehicle's navigation route.

The target trajectories to be generated are represented as a state tensor $\boldsymbol{x}^{(t)} \in \mathbb{R}^{(M+1) \times \tau \times 4}$ at diffusion timestep $t \in [0, 1]$. Here, $M$ is the number of nearby vehicles considered ($M+1$ vehicles including ego vehicle $i=0$), and $\tau$ is the number of future prediction steps. For each agent $i$ at step $k$, the clean target state ($t=0$) consists of a 4D vector containing position coordinates $(p_{x,i}^k, p_{y,i}^k)$, heading yaw angle $\theta_i^k$, and velocity information.

In the forward process of the diffusion model, Gaussian noise is gradually added to the clean trajectory tensor $\boldsymbol{x}^{(0)}$ according to a linear noise schedule, eventually transforming it into standard Gaussian noise $\boldsymbol{x}^{(1)}$. During training, taking the noisy tensor $\boldsymbol{x}^{(t)}$, diffusion timestep $t$, and scene features $\mathbf{E_{f}}$ as input, the model $\mu_\theta(\boldsymbol{x}^{(t)}, t, \mathbf{E_{f}})$ optimizes its parameters to reconstruct the original clean sample $\boldsymbol{x}^{(0)}$.

sections.heading: High-Precision Planning with the SSDS Decoder and DAPSE Guidance
sections.summary: We explain the structure of the SSDS-DiT decoder, which deeply and symmetrically fuses scene information from the initial stage. In addition, we introduce the mathematical derivation of DAPSE, a novel inference-time guidance method that injects arbitrary constraints in the clean trajectory space without expensive auxiliary networks or approximation errors.
sections.details:
### 4.1 Scene Encoder
To effectively integrate diverse multi-modal information from the driving environment, agent histories and lane features are processed with MLP-Mixer blocks, mixing feature dimensions and sequence dimensions independently. Static obstacles are processed by an MLP. Concatenated tokens are passed through self-attention and an FFN to obtain unified context $\mathbf{E_{f}}$. The navigation route is encoded separately and added to diffusion timestep embeddings to form the modulation signal for Adaptive Layer Norm (adaLN) in each layer.

### 4.2 Single-Stream Dual-Stream (SSDS) Decoder
Inspired by modern video generation models, trajectory tokens $\boldsymbol{x}^{(0)}$ and context tokens $\mathbf{E_{f}}$ are treated as two independent streams. In the dual-stream block, both streams undergo separate adaLN modulation and QKV projections, but Q, K, and V are concatenated to perform a single Joint Attention. This enables symmetric information exchange from early stages while preserving modality-specific representations. Subsequently, the single-stream stage fully unifies all tokens into one for deep fusion. Compared to asymmetric, late cross-attention in conventional DiT decoders, this models scene-trajectory interactions much more densely.

### 4.3 DAPSE: Decoupled Annealing Posterior Sampling with Energy
For a pretrained trajectory distribution $q_0(\boldsymbol{x}^{(0)})$, one often wants to sample from a target distribution $p_0(\boldsymbol{x}^{(0)}) \propto q_0(\boldsymbol{x}^{(0)}) \exp(-\beta \mathcal{E}_0(\boldsymbol{x}^{(0)}))$ that minimizes an arbitrary energy function $\mathcal{E}_0(\boldsymbol{x}^{(0)})$ (e.g., target speed tracking). However, exact gradient computation at intermediate noise steps is difficult. Training auxiliary networks hinders real-time execution (10–20 Hz), and existing DPS (Diffusion Posterior Sampling) only holds as an approximation near $t \approx 0$.

Therefore, the authors proposed DAPSE, extending the DAPS framework. By decoupling adjacent noise levels through the clean data manifold and formulating the posterior via Bayes' rule, they derived an inner MCMC update rule using Langevin dynamics under a Gaussian assumption around the current estimated clean trajectory $\hat{\boldsymbol{x}}^{(0)}$. This allows energy gradients to be applied directly in clean sample space rather than in noisy space, achieving high-precision zero-shot trajectory guidance that can correct global estimation errors in early steps.

sections.heading: Turning the Diffusion Model into an Adversary: Closed-Loop Critical Scenario Generation
sections.summary: To test the planner, the same diffusion model is repurposed as a trajectory generator for adversarial agents. In a closed-loop environment, a mechanism was constructed to synthesize realistic yet severe scenarios using energy functions such as lead-time TTC, lane changing, hard braking, and drivable-area compliance.
sections.details:
### 5.1 Closed-Loop Pipeline
The model is integrated into nuPlan's closed-loop environment. Within the simulation, four types of agents exist: (1) the black-box ego planner under test, (2) adversarial agents controlled by the proposed diffusion model, (3) background traffic vehicles following IDM (Intelligent Driver Model), and (4) pedestrians following log playback. At each step, guidance gradients are applied solely to the positional trajectories of adversarial agents. Heading angles are geometrically recomputed from waypoints and tracked with an LQR controller based on a kinematic bicycle model. Because the adversary adapts at every step to the ego vehicle's reactions, realistic interactive hazard behaviors emerge rather than scripted collisions.

### 5.2 Guidance Design Principles
For scenario generation, DPS is adopted to flexibly test various combinations of energy functions. To increase room for trajectory modification, the number of reverse diffusion steps is increased from the conventional 10 steps to 20 steps. A logSNR schedule and DPM-Solver++ allocating more steps to the low-noise regime ($t \in [8 \times 10^{-4}, 0.1]$) are introduced to balance stability and speed. Furthermore, applying gradients directly to positional trajectories rather than velocity or acceleration prevents physical breakdown and allows natural acceleration, deceleration, and avoidance behaviors to emerge.

### 5.3 Energy Functions for Long-Tail Scenarios
- **Time-to-Collision (TTC) with Temporal Lead**: Standard TTC minimization targets the ego vehicle's current position too aggressively, tending to cause unnatural, unavoidable collisions. Introducing a 'temporal lead $\ell$' that computes TTC between future ego step $k+\ell$ and adversary step $k$ guides natural intercept behaviors that preemptively block the ego vehicle's path.
- **Cut-in**: Triggered by longitudinal distance to the ego vehicle, this energy $\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{lc}}$ minimizes lateral deviation $\delta_{\mathrm{lat}}$ to the center line of the ego vehicle's lane, inducing aggressive lane changes.
- **Lead-Vehicle Braking**: Applying energy $\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{brake}}$ penalizing forward progress beyond target travel distance $s^*(k) = k v^* \Delta t$ induces smooth yet abrupt deceleration.
- **Drivable-Area Compliance**: To prevent running off road boundaries, energy $\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{DA}}$ using an ESDF (Euclidean Signed Distance Field) is added to constrain the vehicle footprint within drivable areas.
- **Combined Scenarios**: Based on distance threshold $d_{\mathrm{comb}}$, composite hazard behaviors—such as hard braking followed by a cut-in, or a cut-in followed immediately by hard braking—are triggered sequentially.

sections.heading: A Leap in Planning Performance and Exposing Planner Weaknesses in Critical Scenarios
sections.summary: Experiments on nuPlan confirmed that the SSDS-DP planner outperforms conventional baselines by up to +14.4 points, demonstrating high data efficiency. On the other hand, under the generated critical scenarios, planners with higher nominal performance experienced sharper score drops, revealing critical weaknesses: relying solely on braking without attempting active lateral evasion.
sections.details:
### 6.1 Experimental Setup
Models were trained with three data volumes: 250K (250,000), 650K (650,000), and 1M (1,000,000) scenarios. They were evaluated on nuPlan's Val14, Test14, and Test14-hard splits under Reactive (R) and Non-Reactive (NR) settings. Comparisons were made between baseline Diffusion Planner (DP) and proposed SSDS-DP. For safety-critical evaluation, 25 scenarios selected from Val14 were used, pitting 1M-trained models against each other.

### 6.2 Planning Performance: SSDS-DP vs. DP
Table 1 shows clear trends. First, SSDS-DP achieved massive score improvements on 'Test14-hard Reactive', where vehicle interactions are crucial: +6.8 points with 250K training and +14.4 points with 650K training. Since the gap narrows in non-reactive settings, the SSDS structure clearly provides dramatic gains in modeling inter-agent dependencies rather than mere trajectory precision. High data efficiency with smaller data volumes was also confirmed (though with 1M data, DP catches up to parity). Qualitative results in Figure 3 also show that SSDS-DP maintains turns along the correct navigation path at intersections where the baseline drifts off.

### 6.3 Validation of DAPSE Guidance
In experiments using target speed maintenance energy, updates via Langevin dynamics and noise reinjection appropriately contracted an overshooting trajectory, guiding it smoothly toward the intended speed profile without unnatural fluctuations.

### 6.4 Stress-Testing Planners with Adversarial Scenarios
In evaluations on combined 'cut-in + braking' scenarios (Table 2), scores for both planners dropped drastically upon introducing adversarial agents, with ego-at-fault collisions surging. Surprisingly, SSDS-DP, which had been superior in nominal driving, suffered a larger score drop than baseline DP. Realism metrics for adversary driving behavior remained comparable to SafeSim, proving that it corners planners within physically plausible bounds rather than via unrealistic ramming.

Detailed log analysis revealed that while DP mitigated or delayed collisions by decisively applying hard braking relatively early, SSDS-DP delayed deceleration onset, leading to rear-end collisions. Even more significantly, a shared weakness among learned planners was exposed: **neither planner took any active evasive action, such as swerving laterally to bypass an obstruction, instead relying exclusively on braking**. In intersection crossing collision scenarios where braking alone cannot avoid impact, both planners collided helplessly.

sections.heading: A New Synthesis of Planning and Evaluation via Traffic Priors
sections.summary: This work demonstrated that a single pretrained diffusion model can function as both a high-performance planner and a scenario generator for rigorous safety evaluation. Revealing that benchmark excellence does not imply robustness in extreme scenarios, it highlights potential as a foundation to accelerate the entire autonomous driving development loop.
sections.details:
This paper presented a unified approach for autonomous driving centered on a single pretrained diffusion model. As a planner, the SSDS structure fundamentally improves scene feature fusion, and DAPSE enables constraint guidance without retraining. As a scenario generator, it successfully induces natural yet severe hazardous events in closed-loop simulations.

A highly suggestive finding of this research is that 'even cutting-edge planners boasting high scores on standard driving benchmarks easily crumble when exposed to controlled safety-critical scenarios'. The fundamental flaw where planners resort purely to passive deceleration without performing active lateral evasion could never have been uncovered through conventional benign log-replay evaluations. By learning a single traffic prior, using it both to drive and to challenge provides a powerful development foundation to genuinely enhance autonomous driving safety.

takeaways: By simply altering the guidance gradient direction of energy functions at inference time on the same trajectory diffusion model, one can seamlessly switch between a rule-following ego planner and a threat-inducing adversarial generator.

The Single-Stream Dual-Stream (SSDS) architecture, inspired by video generation models, enables deeper fusion of scene context and trajectories than conventional DiT, yielding dramatic performance gains especially in interaction-heavy scenes.
Planners that dominate standard nominal benchmarks can crumble under adversarial long-tail scenarios, proving that high benchmark scores do not equate to real-world robustness.
Current state-of-the-art learned planners rely exclusively on linear hard braking during imminent hazards and suffer from a critical flaw: an inability to steer laterally for evasion.
limitations: The selection of base scenes and target adversary agents for generating critical scenarios is done manually based on geometric criteria, meaning unintentional sampling bias cannot be fully ruled out.
At the maximum training scale of 1M scenarios, SSDS-DP's advantage over baseline DP diminishes, leaving model and data scaling laws an ongoing question.
For DAPSE guidance, applying it to complex constraints beyond target speed maintenance (such as collision avoidance) and quantitatively evaluating collision rates and TTC remains future work.
